newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. wants quick fix for Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants quick fix for Mideast peace.

text.p: The United States told Israel and the Palestinians to reach quick, concrete results in talks resuming on Sunday to end blooshed and salvage Washington's Middle East peace strategy.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, dispatched to the region after an emergency PLO-Israeli summit at the White House last week, said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu assured him he would carry out signed agreements with the PLO.
"The recent violence has demonstrated the great urgency of reaching some concrete results just as soon as possible," Christopher told a news conference with Netanyahu.
Afterwards Christopher met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat before the start of talks between teams of lower-level negotiators on the Israeli side of the border with the self-ruled Gaza Strip.

The resumption of these talks was the main achievement of President Bill Clinton's hastily-convened summit to save five years of U.S.-mediated peace talks threatened by violence that killed 58 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers.

Netanyahu, whose opening of a tunnel near Jerusalem's Moslem holy places triggered that violence, said Israel sought a joint recommitment with the Palestinians to their peace accords. But he declined to set a date for a troop redeployment from the West Bank city of Hebron, delayed since March.

"What we seek is a simultaneous recommitment by both sides to the principles that both signed on to in Oslo," he said in a reference to the Palestinian interim self-rule accord launched in 1993 in the Norwegian capital.
Asked about Hebron, Netanyahu, usually fluent before the cameras, awkwardly sidestepped the question.

"I am not putting a date. I'm putting a conclusion. The satisfactory conclusion of the negotiation, I think from both sides, will be the date in which you'll be able to signify as a conclusion. And once it's concluded, I don't think there should be a delay in its implementation," he said in English.
Netanyahu sought to calm Palestinian fears that he wanted to rewrite the Oslo agreement signed by his Labour party predecessors.
"We did not propose opening the agreement. We suggested that within the confines of the existing agreement adjustments be made," he told the news conference.
Netanyahu wants to modify security arrangements for Jewish settlers in Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns to be given self-rule.
Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said if Israel tried to reopen Oslo the PLO could seek international arbitration.
"If the Israeli side is demanding to open the agreement, it seems to me that they are saying we don't have an agreement anymore and let's start from the beginning," Erekat told Reuters.
Arafat has sought international support for his stance. Clinton, four weeks before a presidential election, has been loathe to lean on Netanyahu, but the European Union has sought to play a role.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring left for the Middle East on Sunday. Christopher seemed cool to direct European involvement saying "any major change in the bilateral character of these negotiations is not likely to take place".
Christopher said Netanyahu was committed to moving forward.

"The prime minister assured me that he understands the context of these negotiations is to go forward with the implementation of the interim agreement which he understands there is an obligation to carry out," Christopher said.
"I don't have any doubt that the prime minister understands the urgency of these negotiations," Christopher said, in his usual understated diplomatic language.
Christopher will not take part in the continuous talks at the Erez crossing in Gaza.
Those talks, with the participation of Christopher's Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, centre on Hebron.
